readerTitle: The leak that showed you how your company really works
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (가정용 배관 설치 회사와 B2B 고객인 부동산 관리회사) · 모든 인물, 수치, 상황은 설명용
insight: 고객에게 닿은 품질 사고는 한 사람의 실수가 아니라 프로세스에 대한 증거다. 봉쇄, 원인, 예방, 신뢰 회복 순서로 대응한다.
misconception: 고객 불만 한 건은 그 건만 고치고, 실수한 직원을 주의 주면 끝난다.

sources.text: 품질 관리의 표준 개념 (봉쇄 조치, 근본 원인 분석, 표준화, 실수 방지)
모든 인물, 수치, 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 가상 시나리오입니다. 설치 30건, 누수 3건(첫 신고 1건과 점검에서 발견한 2건), 관리회사 건물 설치 8건 중 누수 2건이 카드 사이에서 일관되는지 확인하세요.
온수기 설치 후 최종 점검(압력 확인, 이음부 누수 확인) 방식은 지역 규정과 제품마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 특정 기준값이나 시간을 쓰지 않고 일반적으로만 표현했습니다.
테이크어웨이의 결정별 개념 매핑(품질 비용, 표준, 실수 방지, 전략으로서의 품질)이 OPS-06 유닛의 각 레슨 내용과 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Monday, 8 a.m. A photo of a puddle.
body: You run a plumbing company with 12 technicians. A customer sends a photo: water pooling under the water heater your team installed on Friday.
Last week your team installed 30 heaters. Eight went into apartments owned by a property manager, your biggest client. The next four decisions are yours.

image.label: Phone showing a photo of water under a water heater
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침 사무실 책상 위 스마트폰 화면에 온수기 아래 물웅덩이 사진이 떠 있고, 옆에 식은 커피잔. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What's your first move?
body: The customer is upset but polite. You don't yet know if this leak is a one-off.

options.text: Send a technician today, fix it and apologize
options.feedback: The visible problem is solved fast. But if the cause isn't unique, other homes may leak later, and each one costs more once it soaks a floor.

options.text: Fix this one, then call all 30 customers from last week and offer a free check
options.feedback: It costs a day of checks. In return you find problems while they're cheap drips, not ruined floors and angry reviews.

options.text: Fix this one and wait to see if more complaints come in
options.feedback: You save a day now. But you let customers become your inspectors, and they'll find the next leak at the worst moment.

cards.title: Three technicians, three ways to check.
body: Say you chose the free checks. They find two more slow leaks, from two different technicians.
You ask how each person does the final check. One watches the joints for a minute. One runs a pressure test. One checks "if there's time." What do you conclude?

options.text: Two technicians were careless. Give them a formal warning
options.feedback: It feels decisive, but nobody ever told them what the check should be. The next new hire will guess too.

options.text: There's no shared standard. Write one: what to test, how, and what counts as a pass
options.feedback: You fix the gap that let three people do the job three ways. It takes an afternoon and some arguing with your senior techs.

options.text: Ask your most senior technician to spot-check new installs
options.feedback: You'll catch some leaks, but one person can't see every job, and you still haven't defined what "good" is.

cards.title: How do you make it stick on a busy Friday?
body: Say you wrote the standard: a one-page final check every technician agrees on.
The leaks happened on rushed afternoons. How do you make sure the check happens when people are tired and behind?

options.text: Email the standard and repeat it at the weekly meeting
options.feedback: Easy and free. But reminders fade within weeks, and rushed afternoons don't.

options.text: Add a "final check done" box to the job checklist
options.feedback: A checklist helps memory. But a box can be ticked without doing the test.

options.text: Make the job app refuse to close a job until a photo of the pressure reading is uploaded
options.feedback: Skipping the check becomes hard and visible. It costs about a minute per job and a few grumbles.

cards.title: Your biggest client wants answers.
body: Say you added the photo step. Then an email arrives from the property manager's operations lead: "Two of these leaks were in our buildings. What happened?"
She has to explain it to the building owners.

options.text: Apologize briefly and say it was a one-off
options.feedback: Short and comfortable. But it wasn't a one-off, and if another leak happens, your word stops counting.

options.text: Explain what failed, what you checked, what you changed, and offer the pressure photo for every future job in her buildings
options.feedback: You admit an uncomfortable gap. In return she gets proof she can pass upward, and you become the safer vendor.
Money softens the moment. It doesn't answer her real question: will this happen again?

cards.title: A failure is evidence about the process.
body: Look at the four calls together. You **contained** the damage, found the **cause in the process** rather than a person, **prevented** a repeat, then **rebuilt trust** with proof.
The first leak wasn't really the problem. It was the one customer who happened to notice a gap every job had.
cards.softwareNote: A bug that reaches users follows the same path: warn affected users before they report it, ask why the tests missed it, then add an automated check that blocks the release until it passes.

cards.title: Don't turn every slip into a new rule.
body: A full response costs time. A truly random slip, like one dropped part, may only need a fix and a note.
New steps also go stale. A photo can become a ritual nobody looks at, so spot-check a few each month.
And "fix the process" doesn't excuse someone who knew the standard and ignored it. That's a different conversation.

image.label: A thick rulebook next to a single simple checklist
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 먼지 쌓인 두꺼운 규정집, 오른쪽에 한 장짜리 체크리스트와 압력계 사진이 담긴 스마트폰. 오른쪽이 더 밝게 조명됨. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Contain, find the cause, prevent, then prove it.
body: Each call in this story used one idea from this unit:
list: **Free checks:** the cost of poor quality grows the later a failure is found
**One written check:** standards turn guesses into a shared definition of good
**Photo before closing:** mistake-proofing makes the right step the easy step
**Honest account to the client:** quality, shown with proof, becomes a reason to choose you
cards.callout: **Try it today:** pick your last customer complaint. Ask whether the same gap could exist in other jobs you haven't heard about yet.
